column1: # Guard regression cases. Columns: guard <TAB> fixture <TAB> command <TAB> expected
# Every spelling here was taken from alxjrvs's own session transcripts or from a
# reproduction during the 2026-07-25 audit. Cases marked REGRESSION failed on the
# pre-fix guards; they are the reason this suite exists.
# fixture:  primary (on main) | wt-a (up to date w/ main) | wt-c (stacked on feature-b) | nonrepo
# --- rebase-guard: direct push to the default branch ------------------------
# REGRESSION: `--dry-run` anywhere in the command disabled the whole guard, so a
# real push to main was ALLOWED because an unrelated commit message contained it.

column3: git commit -m "test --dry-run flag" && git push origin main
git commit -m "document --dry-run" && git push origin HEAD:main

column1: # A genuine dry run still passes — it never mutates the remote.
# --- rebase-guard: must NOT fire out of turn --------------------------------
# REGRESSION: the word "main" inside a commit message denied a push of a
# perfectly ordinary feature branch. This is the false positive alxjrvs reported.

column3: git commit -m "push to main branch when ready" && git push origin feature-a
git commit -m "merge into main later" && git push origin feature-a

column1: # Not a real push/pr-create at all.
# REGRESSION: `--base` was ignored, so a stacked PR was told to rebase onto main,
# which would flatten the stack `rebase-prs` deliberately builds.
# With no --base it really is behind origin/HEAD, so denying is correct.
# All of these were ALLOWED by the pre-fix guard, reproduced through this very
# harness. The suite had grown from two past incidents, so it tested THE FIXES
# rather than THE RULE — and the rule has many more spellings than the rule's
# The single highest-value miss: the natural agent spelling. `HEAD` is not the
# literal string `main`, and two positionals meant it wasn't a "bare" push.
# A `#` comment is not a dry run. This is the 2026-07-25 incident in a new
# spelling: the old `case " $push_seg " in *" --dry-run "*` scanned the segment
# as text, so anything after a comment marker still disabled the guard.
# Last-push-wins: `push_seg=$seg` overwrote, so only the FINAL push segment was
# ever examined and the real push ahead of it was never seen.

column3: git push origin main && git push origin main --dry-run

column1: # Quoting. The destination regex required a whitespace/EOL/separator boundary
# after the branch name, and a quote is none of those.
# Refspec spellings. `+main` force-pushes main; the optional `([^[:space:]]*:)?`
# group required a trailing colon, so a leading `+` was never absorbed.
# `pushargs=${push_seg#*push}` stripped through the FIRST literal "push", which
# `-c push.default=…` supplies — leaving ".default=current push" to tokenize.
# Shell constructs: `prog` was `(git`, `then`, `do` — never the bare token `git`.

column3: if true; then git push origin main; fi
for i in 1; do git push origin main; done

column1: # Wrappers, env prefixes and absolute paths. Claude Code's own matcher strips
# these before matching; this guard tokenizes independently and stripped none.
# A TRAILING `cd` retargeted GIT() at a non-repo AFTER the push was matched, so
# the guard fell through its own fail-open path. Only a `cd` that precedes the
# push can change which repo is pushed.
# `git -C <path>` names the repo being pushed just as surely as a leading `cd`,
# but the flag-skipping loop discarded its value, so the guard judged every
# cross-repo push against the SESSION's cwd repo instead of the target.
# Found bootstrapping a brand-new empty repo: `git -C ~/Code/butter push` was
# denied with "Branch is behind origin/main" — true of the dotFiles checkout the
# session happened to be sitting in, and meaningless for a remote that had no
# branches at all. Both directions are wrong, and the second one is the one that
#   FALSE DENY  — a legitimate push blocked by an unrelated repo's staleness,
#                 which makes bootstrapping any new repo impossible in-session.
#   FALSE ALLOW — the default-branch rule resolves `origin/HEAD` from the cwd
#                 repo too, so a push to another repo's default is judged
#                 against the wrong default, and a non-repo cwd fails open and
# REGRESSION — `-C` is not `cd`, and conflating them opened a hole worse than the bug the
# original -C handling closed. `cd` persists across `&&` segments; `-C` binds to the one
# invocation carrying it. Honouring a `-C` from an EARLIER segment retargeted the guard at that
# directory, where the is-inside-work-tree probe fails, so a bare push to the default branch
# FAILED OPEN. Measured against the shipped guard: all four of the deny cases below were ALLOWED.
# The first two are the bypass proper: an inert `-C` on a non-push segment must not move the
# judgement. The next two are the other half — a `-C` on the push itself DOES name the repo git
# will act on, so a cross-repo push to another checkout's default branch has to be judged against
# THAT repo, cumulatively and relative to any preceding `cd`, exactly as git resolves it.

column3: git -C ../nonrepo status && git push origin main
git -C ../nonrepo log && git push origin main
cd .. && git -C primary push origin main

column1: # …and the inert `-C` must stay inert in the ALLOW direction too, or the fix is just a
# blanket-deny wearing a bypass fix's clothes.

column3: git -C ../nonrepo status && git push origin feature-x
git -C ../nonrepo status && git -C ../primary push origin feature-x

column1: # Heredoc bodies are DATA, not command structure. Writing the commit message for
# this very change was DENIED by the guard because the message explained
# `git push origin main`. Prose apostrophes ("lefthook's") also unbalance the
# quote tracking, so a heredoc cannot be parsed as if it were shell text.
# `\n` is expanded to a real newline by run.sh.

column3: git commit -F - << 'MSG'\nexplain git push origin main here\nMSG

git commit -F - << 'MSG'
lefthook's guard denied this
git push origin main
MSG
gh pr create --body - << 'EOF'\nthis PR changes git push origin main\nEOF

column1: # A herestring has no body and must NOT swallow the rest of the command.

column3: grep -q x <<< "text" ; git push origin main

column1: # A newline separates simple commands exactly as `;` does. Without this the whole
# multi-line command collapsed into one segment and the push was never seen.
# Redirections are not refspecs, and must not shift the positional analysis.
# FALSE POSITIVES: the guard denied real work because segmentation ignored
# quoting. The first spelling denied an actual tool call during the audit.

column3: git commit -m "run cd . && git push origin main to ship"
git commit -m "see 'git push origin main' in the docs"

column1: # --- op-guard: the shapes an agent MUST be able to use ----------------------
# This whole block is the point of the 2026-08-18 change. Every one of these was
# DENIED by the old binary-scoped `Bash(op:*)` rule, including `op --version`,
# which prints no secret at all. `op run --` is 1Password's own documented shape:
# "If a subprocess used with op run prints a secret to stdout, the secret will be
# `op item list` and `op item move` are now ALLOWED, and the reason the guard used
# to give for excluding them no longer holds: it said inventory browsing "is not
# what was asked for". It has since been asked for, with a named use — the vault
# audit reports an undeclared item and moving it out is how you fix it.
# Both print titles and metadata, never a secret VALUE, which is this guard's
# actual criterion. `op vault list` and `op account list` stay DENIED: the measured
# exposure recorded for them is enumerating every vault in the ACCOUNT via the
# desktop integration, far outside claude-agent, which is a different capability.
# `op item move` is allowed in ONE DIRECTION. Moving an item OUT of the agent vault
# can only narrow the agent's own reach. Moving one IN widens it — that is a
# self-escalation path: an agent could grant itself a production credential by
# relocating it into the vault its service account reads. Outbound allowed, inbound

column3: op item move render-api-key --current-vault claude-agent --destination-vault Archive
op item move prod-db --current-vault Prod --destination-vault claude-agent

column1: # The interpreter and `op run --` trampolines must not launder an inbound move past
# the direction check, the same way they must not launder `op read`.

column3: op run -- op item move prod-db --destination-vault claude-agent

column1: # Reading and destroying stay denied regardless of the widening above.
# Global flags must be skipped to reach the subcommand, or `--format` would eat
# the verb and `op --format json read op://x` would resolve its subcommand to `json`.
# `op inject` is safe ONLY when it writes to a file instead of stdout.
# op-agent is plumbing, but its one non-printing verb is the health check that
# `boom verify` runs; an agent debugging the secret path needs it.
# --- op-guard: `op plugin`, the biometric path for HUMAN CLIs ---------------
# Shell plugins are 1Password's answer to a CLI token sitting in plaintext on
# disk: the credential lives in the vault and is released per-invocation behind
# Touch ID. Every discovery verb here was DENIED by the default-deny arm, which
# is the same failure mode the 2026-08-18 rewrite was written to end — the guard
# blocked the vendor's recommended pattern, so the advice became "run it from
# your own terminal". `list`, `inspect` and `clear` print configuration metadata
# only; `init` is an interactive picker that prints a `source` line. None emits a
# credential VALUE, which is this guard's actual criterion.
# `op plugin run` is the ONE plugin verb that injects a live credential into a
# child process, so it gets the identical vetting as `op run --` rather than a
# pass — same `--`, same env-dumping children, same interpreter payloads, and
# the same 2026-08-19 trampoline finding: `op run -- op read` was allowed for
# months because the guard saw an unremarkable child, and `op plugin run -- op
# `gh` is DENIED as a plugin-run child, and this is the guard stating a
# conclusion rather than an omission. `_bad_op_run_child` rejects `git`/`gh`
# under any injecting invocation because rebase-guard.sh tokenizes for a
# `git`/`gh` PROGRAM and sees `op` here — so `op plugin run -- gh pr merge`
# would walk a merge past the push guards. It costs nothing: gh resolves its
# token from the keychain via `gh auth git-credential`, never from a plugin.
# A gh shell plugin on this machine would be a THIRD GitHub credential path
# beside that and `op-agent git-credential`, and its alias lives in an
# interactive-shell `plugins.sh` an agent never sources — so it would break
# agent `gh` while adding a credential. The deny is the recommendation.

column3: op plugin run -- gh repo list
op plugin run -- op read op://claude-agent/x/credential
op plugin run -- op-agent secret op://claude-agent/x/credential
op plugin run gh repo list

column1: # `op plugin run -- git push` would hide the push from rebase-guard.sh for the
# same reason `op run -- git push` does: both guards tokenize for a `git` PROGRAM

column3: op plugin run -- git push origin main

column1: # The interpreter and `op run --` trampolines must not launder a plugin-run
# child past the vetting above. This is why `plugin` had to join _OP_VERB_RE.

column3: op run -- op plugin run -- env

# Prose about plugins is still ordinary work — the false positive this suite exists for.

column3: git commit -m "wire op plugin run for vercel"

# command. A `git` segment is never substring-scanned, so a commit message about

git commit -m "op read is denied; use op run --"
echo "op read is the denied shape"

column1: # Word-boundary, not substring: none of these contain an `op` command.
# --- op-guard: values on stdout stay denied ---------------------------------
# stdout is model context. These are the paths with a confirmed incident.
# Bare `op inject` renders the template, secrets and all, to STDOUT.
# Masking is the property that makes `op run` safe; the flag that removes it
# converts the allowed shape back into a printing one.
# A child whose whole job is to print the environment defeats masking.
# REGRESSION-BY-CONSTRUCTION: `op run -- git push` would hide the push from
# rebase-guard.sh, which tokenizes for a `git` PROGRAM and sees `op` here.

column3: op run -- git push origin main

column1: # No `--` means the guard cannot tell which words are the child command.
# `op-agent header` is the exact command that put a live PAT into a transcript
# `audit` prints titles and a verdict, never a field value — but it is still
# denied from a Bash tool call, like every op-agent verb except the (also
# unreachable) `status`. Its only consumer is a `boom verify` run step, which
# spawns op-agent as a boom child and so never reaches the permission system.
# This case locks that in: adding a verb must not widen the Bash surface.
# --- op-guard: `op run --` must not trampoline back into op --------------------
# git/gh, but not `op` itself — so `op run -- op read op://…` was ALLOWED by the
# guard and unmatched by `permissions.deny` (whose rules anchor on `op read` as
# the first token, not `op run -- op read`). `Bash(op run:*)` is in
# permissions.allow, so the shape was pre-approved. Masking does not help: it
# conceals values `op run` injected, and a self-reading child injected nothing.

column3: op run -- op item get claude-git-pat
op run -- op item edit x --title y

column1: # Path spellings resolve because the child is basenamed before the check.
# CONTROLS — the legitimate shape must keep working, or this fix is an outage.
# --- op-guard: the spellings `permissions.deny` structurally cannot cover ----
# CLAUDE.md: deny matches command SPELLING, so an absolute path is not covered,
# and "deny cannot cover an arbitrary interpreter — sh -c 'op read …' still walks
# past". The guard takes a basename and scans interpreter payloads, so both are.
# `_norm` strips a leading `env` / assignment, so neither disguises the program.
# Segmentation: a denied verb anywhere in a compound command is still denied.
# REGRESSION (2026-08-28 audit): op-guard treats an interpreter as the residue
# `permissions.deny` cannot cover and scans its payload. rebase-guard never got
# the same treatment, so the identical shape reached a push to main. `sudo git
# push` is absent from this block deliberately — the shared `_norm` fix in the
# previous commit already closed it for every guard at once, which is the whole
# `git -c alias.X=push X` — the flag loop consumed `-c alias.yolo=push` as a
# value-taking global and then read the subcommand as `yolo`, so the push was
# never recognised as a push at all. The alias is not resolved, it is refused:
# resolving it would mean running `git config` from inside a guard.
# An interpreter payload that pushes somewhere SAFE is still allowed — the fix
# expands the payload so the ordinary refspec logic judges it, rather than
# The false positive this suite exists for: a commit message naming a push is
# prose, not a command, and no expansion may reach inside one.

column3: git commit -m "explain git push origin main in the docs"

column1: # REGRESSION (2026-08-28 audit): every row below was ALLOWED by the guard that
# passed 156/156. Four holes in one family, none of them reachable by
# `permissions.deny`, whose rules anchor `op read` as the FIRST token:
#   1. `_split` had no `$( )` / backtick / `<( )` handling, so a substitution
#      body was never tokenized as a command at all.
#   2. `_norm`'s assignment arm shifted past `X=$(op`, resolving the program
#   4. `_is_interpreter` listed shells but no scripting runtime, so any
#      language with a `system()` was an open door.
# The substitution rows are the important ones: a value on stdout IS the leak,
# and command substitution is the shortest path to putting one there.
# `op run --` may not trampoline through a scripting interpreter either. The
# child prints the injected environment, which is the masking argument defeated
# exactly as `env`/`printenv` would — those were listed, these were not.
# A substitution that is NOT an op command stays allowed — the fix widens the
# tokenizer, it does not widen the verdict.
# --- op-guard: allow-list means UNKNOWN fails closed ------------------------
# This is the inversion the change is built on. Under the old deny-list a verb
# nobody enumerated sailed through — that is exactly how `op-agent header`, the
# one command with a confirmed leak, stayed reachable. Destructive and
# not-yet-invented verbs now fail the same closed way as the printing ones.
# --- REGRESSION: a newline INSIDE quotes is data, not a separator -------------
# Found by this suite's own author being unable to commit. `_split` correctly keeps
# a quoted newline in one segment, but the segment list is NEWLINE-DELIMITED, so
# every consumer's `while read` re-split it — and a commit message with a line
# beginning `op read ...` arrived at the guard looking like an `op` invocation.
# This is the same class the heredoc cases above cover, reached by a different
# road: `-m` prose rather than a heredoc body. A quoted `;` was already handled,
# which is what made the gap invisible — the quote tracking was never broken, the

column3: git commit -m "a change\n\nop read op://x/y is denied because it prints values"
git commit -m "notes\nop item get stays denied"

column3: git commit -m "why we avoid\ngit push origin HEAD:main"

# narrowed the split to quoted newlines rather than disabling newline splitting.
# (rebase-guard's `git status\ngit push origin main` already asserts the same thing
# further up — not repeated here, since a duplicate case adds no coverage and only

# --- REGRESSION: a quoted or expanded PROGRAM name -------------------------
# `_norm` compared and emitted the program token RAW, so one pair of quotation
# marks resolved the program name to `"op"` — which is not `op` — and every
# guard sourcing guard-lib.sh waved the command through. `"op" read` put a live
# credential on stdout: the exact 2026-07-25 leak the allow-list exists to make
# structurally impossible. All seven of these were ALLOWED before the fix.
# A program name that is itself a shell expansion cannot be read statically, so
# it is refused rather than waved through — same doctrine as an unknown verb.
# MUST STILL ALLOW: quoting a SANCTIONED spelling stays sanctioned. The fix
# resolves the name; it does not deny quoting.
# MUST STILL ALLOW: a `$` inside an ARGUMENT is not a program name. Only the
# program token is refused when unreadable, or every command with a variable in
# MUST STILL ALLOW: a substitution inside an ARGUMENT is a path or prose, not a
# program name. Denying these would recreate the commit-message false positive.
# MUST STILL ALLOW, multi-line: `^` is a LINE anchor in grep, so before the
# quote-state fix every line start of a multi-line argument read as program
# position. A markdown code fence inside a PR body — a line beginning with a
# backtick — was denied as a substituted program name. Measured three times in
# one session, none of them invoking 1Password. The fence is INSIDE an open
# MUST STILL DENY, multi-line: a newline IS a command separator when it is not
# inside a quote or a heredoc body, so a substituted program name on the second
# line is still program position. This is the case the fix must not widen past.
# --- REGRESSION: `git push --all` / `--mirror` from a feature branch --------
# Both name their refs from the local ref namespace, not from argv, so the
# refspec analysis could not see them and they fell through to "pushes the
# CURRENT branch" — which from wt-a reads as safe. `--all` pushes every local
# branch including the default one; `--mirror` also DELETES remote refs absent
# locally. Both were ALLOWED before this fix.
# MUST STILL ALLOW: a dry run never mutates the remote, even with --all.
# MUST STILL ALLOW: an ordinary feature-branch push is untouched.
# --- REGRESSION: a pipe character inside a QUOTED argument is prose ---------
# Both scans read the raw command, so a `|` inside a quoted string counted as a
# shell operator and these were DENIED — the exact commit-message false
# positive this suite exists to prevent, reopened by the gate meant to keep it
# closed. It blocked read-only work three times during the 2026-08-28 audit,
# including the writing of the finding that describes it.

git commit -m 'doc: the |bash pipe walks past op read op://x'

column1: # MUST STILL DENY: an UNQUOTED pipe into an interpreter is a real shell
# operator, and the payload it carries is exactly what this gate is for.
# --- op-guard: command runners, and boom's own askpass ----------------------
# REGRESSION (2026-08-28 audit). Two holes, one shape: the guard resolves a
# program name and dispatches on it, so anything that RUNS a program without
# being one of the wrappers `_norm` strips reaches the real command unread.
# 1. `boom askpass <ref>` resolves a secret ref to stdout — it is in boom's own
#    --help — and `boom` was in no deny rule and no guard arm. The allow-list
#    architecture in op-guard.sh exists because "a deny-list of verbs missed the
#    one verb that leaked"; this was a fourth spelling of the same leak, in the
#    binary this repo drives on every sync.
# 2. Development-environment runners. Claude Code's built-in wrapper list is
#    fixed and documents that `mise exec`, `npx`, `devbox run` and `docker exec`
#    are NOT in it, so `permissions.deny` cannot see past them either. Both
#    layers missed the same eight spellings.
# boom's read-only verbs are how the machine is actually driven — denying these
# would make the guard unusable, which is the failure mode that got a
# The runners. `--` present and absent, since neither form is required.
# Positive controls: the runners themselves are ordinary commands and must not
# become undeniable just because they appear in a command line.
# --- op-guard: the two secret-printers with no path-spelling sibling --------
# `Bash(*/op *)` and `Bash(*/op-agent *)` so a path spelling cannot walk past a
# name-anchored rule. Two entries never got that treatment:
#   Bash(security find-generic-password:*)  — guards the SERVICE-ACCOUNT TOKEN,
#     which reads every item in the vault. The single highest-value secret on
#     the machine sat behind the weakest rule in the list.
#   Bash(git credential:*)                  — the helper chain ends at
#     `op-agent git-credential`, which prints `password=<PAT>` on stdout, so
#     `git credential fill` hands the model a live PAT. Same class as the
#     2026-07-25 `op-agent header` incident, through a different door.
# op-guard never woke for either: its bail-out regex excludes `-` after `op`, so
# `op-claude-agent` never matched, and it had no `security` or `git` arm at all.
# Positive controls: `security` and `git` are ordinary commands. Denying them
# wholesale would break the machine — only the credential-printing verbs go.
# --- op-guard: the runner arms, second pass -------------------------------
# REGRESSION (pre-merge review of the first pass). The arms added above shipped
# four defects of their own, all found by measurement rather than reading:
#   npm exec / npm x / docker exec had no arm at all — same shape, installed.
#   `mise exec <tool> -- CMD` broke out early unless the tool spec carried an `@`,
#     so `mise exec rg -- op read` resolved its program to `rg`. The only case
#     covering it used `node@20`, which passed for the wrong reason.
#   caffeinate/arch/setsid/chroot shared one flag list across four incompatible
#     grammars: `-w` takes an argument for caffeinate and NONE for setsid, arch's
#     `-d`/`-e` were absent, and chroot's mandatory newroot operand was never
#     skipped, so that arm could not reach a command on any platform.
#   `npx -c '<command string>'` skipped its argument as if it were a flag's, which
#     hid the command rather than failing to read it.
# Each row below was `allow` before the second pass.
# The same shapes must not reach a default-branch push either — the arms live in
# guard-lib.sh, so rebase-guard inherits every one of them.

column3: npm exec -- git push origin main
arch -d FOO git push origin main
docker exec box git push origin main

column1: # Positive controls: every runner is an ordinary command in its ordinary shape.
# --- op-guard: the bail-out must not swallow ordinary commands --------------
# REGRESSION (same review). Widening the bail-out to wake on the bare program
# names `boom`, `security` and `git` dragged every ordinary git command into this
# guard's two unconditional deny paths — the one for a program name that comes
# from a command substitution, and the one for a name it cannot statically read.
# Measured: these five were `allow` before the widening and DENY after it, and the
# fourth is boom's actual install path on this machine. The bail-out is anchored on
# the SUBCOMMAND now, so the guard never sees them.
# …while the subcommands that DO print a credential still wake it, by every
